Evan

Degrees of freedom for the chi-square test is not equivalent to the number of detections.

Degrees of freedom for such a test is described in slide 6 from the introductory distance sampling workshop:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch2/L2-1%20Assessment%20of%20Model%20Performance.pdf

In your situation, "u" (the number of distance categories) is 4. I can't guess the number of parameters in your mrmodel where you have two categorical variables (multiplied?) plus an interaction of size (discrete or continuous?) and distance. I'm  certain that model has buckets more parameters than 4. It is true that ddf.gof​ should have not calculated a negative number of degrees of freedom, and simply reported that a test could not be performed.

However, I have some doubt about that mrmodel​ you have tried to fit. I'm skeptical that the parameters in that model are estimable. It seems an odd model, not something I've come across previously (an interaction without a main effect). Have you looked at the parameter estimates coming from the ddf​ output? I think the ddf.gof()​ is trying to warn you of a possibly deeper problem; non-convergence. I suggest a simpler model.

P.S. I don't do anything special to get well behaved cut-and-paste from RStudio. Note I'm taking code from the editor window, rather than the console. Cut and paste from the console is messier. My email client asks when I attempt to paste something from the console if I want to paste with or without formatting. Maybe that's the secret.

Gemma, you don’t clarify how you estimate abundance from your second method.  By ‘singular fixed observation point’, do you mean an attempt at a complete count of animals from a point that gives you a view of the whole area of interest?  i.e. a vantage point count?  But you then apply a detection function to correct that count?  I am not clear how that would work.  Point transect methods cannot be applied when you record for several hours from a point, as animal movement will generate substantial upward bias in any abundance estimate.  And the method needs a design with a number of points – you cannot get valid inference if you have a single observation point. You don’t give any details to know whether issues like responsive movement away from observers, non-random selection of points, or failure to detect animals very close to a point could be occurring.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Gemma

Thanks for replying to Steve's request for further details. Your vantage point counts suffer from positive bias arising from animal movement. As duration of a count increases, animals in the course of their affairs, will move. Random movement causes positive bias in estimates because animals that move toward the vantage point will be included in the detections while animals moving away are less likely to be detected. This has been demonstrated by Glennie et al. (2015)
Glennie, R., Buckland, S. T., and Thomas, L. (2015), The Effect of Animal Movement on Line Transect Estimates of Abundance, PLoS One, 10, e0121333

Regarding your thermal point transect surveys. You note the detections were made along tracks and badgers are either attracted or repelled by the tracks. In either event, badgers know where the point transects are located hence distribution of badgers with respect to the thermal detector is being confounded with the estimated shape of the detection function.

One of our colleagues developed a method to disentangle the two distributions when conducting point counts along roads (in your neck of the woods).
Marques, T. A., Buckland, S. T., Borchers, D. L., Tosh, D., & McDonald, R. A. (2010). Point transect sampling along linear features. Biometrics, 66, 1247–1255.  https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x

but it requires the collection of additional data and there is no "off-the-shelf" software to conduct such an analysis.

I'm afraid that doesn't exactly resolve your problems, but it does highlight the difficulties of the issue.

Good day Emeline,

Sorry, there is a lot here and I didn't have time to respond right away.

Your questions concern several different issues, including
1. Potentially long and variable camera recovery times , such that t  (the time interval between snapshot moments at which images could be recorded) is unknown and must be estimated. Recovery times result from imperfect and variable performance of cameras.
2. Potentially long and variable "retrigger times" for animals that remain stationary within the field of view. This can cause animals to be missed when in the FOV at snapshot moments ("false negatives"), and hence negative bias in the encounter rate . Long or variable retrigger times are caused by animal behaviour (staying still for a few to several seconds), so are likely to be species-specific.
3. Reactions to cameras.
4. Estimating activity level with respect to your (daily) survey duration
5. Detections of animals in groups

The article you mentioned addresses only 1 and 2 above, though reactions to cameras and activity level are also relevant.

Some specific responses inline below. Steve and others please feel free to correct me or add to my comments.

>    Kühl, H. S., Buckland, S. T., Henrich, M., Howe, E., & Heurich, M. (2023). Estimating effective survey duration in camera trap distance sampling surveys. Ecology and Evolution, 13, e10599. https://doi.org/10.1002/ ece3.10599
>
> First, congratulations for this great article that made me question how I calculated my camera trap survey effort in the case of still images.
>
> We have finalized a big camera trap survey in Cambodia in one of our protected areas and I managed to calculate population estimates for 5 species and I just finished estimating distances for 2 other species:
> - 2 squirrels species and one treeshrew
> - 1 junglefowl species
> - 1 pheasant species
> - wild pig (population estimate currently being estimated)
> - 1 macaque species (population estimate currently being estimated)
>
> I would like to recalculate the survey effort following the methodology described in the article and see how it affects our population estimates. For the two squirrels and the treeshrew, no behavioural reaction of the animal to cameras were observed. In this case, can I use the experimentally derived camera recovery time or do you still recommend to calculate the effective survey duration for each species based on our dataset given that other factors can also potentionally influence the camera recovery time?

EJH: This is consistent with this recommendation from the article: "If it is clear, for example from prior surveys that there are no behavioural reactions of animals to cameras, retrigger delays from natural behaviour are negligible and experimentally derived camera recovery time shows little variation under different conditions, it  should be sufficient to just use the experimentally derived value for t."

>
> For the other species, reaction to cameras was observed. The time interval data should therefore be manually inspected for each of those 4 species.

EJH: Yes, to avoid bias when modelling the detection function and estimating encounter rate and abundance, detections in which animals react to cameras should be censored. See https://peerj.com/articles/13510/ and the article Dr. Palencia recommended.
Data from reactive animals are potentially informative about recovery times, but potentially misleading with respect to retrigger times. If animals remain in the FOV and move sufficiently to retrigger the camera while reacting, times between consecutive triggers are informative about camera recovery times. However the same animal behaving normally (not reacting) might move less and so the retrigger times for observations included in the data would be longer than for reacting animals. For this reason, I might recommend first censoring observations of animals reacting to cameras before estimating t from the data.

> I would first need to clean a bit the dataset for each species and remove any images where I have other species on the images (we did see sometimes wild pig and pheasant or junglefowl on the same images, so these photos should be removed from the dataset).

EJH: Sorry, I'm not sure it's necessary to censor these data when modelling the detection function or estimating encounter rates and abundance, but species-specific retrigger times would be affected.

> This is where I am not fully sure about the next step. From what I understood, I need to filter for only those pictures belonging to the same animal to get a ‘clean’ time interval distribution that is not contaminated with time intervals between pictures belonging to different animals.

EJH: You could, and this was the approach we took with the "checked dataset" subset of the data, (see section 2.4) but you don't necessarily need to. That's the advantage of the methods described in the article. From section 2.3:
"A direct approach to estimating t would be to examine consecutive images, determine whether successive detections are of the same individual and simply take the sample mean of the intervals between successive detections. However, this requires a lot of time and effort to track an individual within one passage through the field of view and to record the intervals within such a series. By contrast, a statistical approach to derive non-observation times (hereby referred to as ‘mean time intervals between triggers’) from time interval distribution data gives results very quickly."

> I have in my record table the number of individuals recorded on images, especially for wild pig where we can have images with 7 individuals. Do I then need to first remove those images from the dataset (images with number of individuals higher than 1), and then look through the rest of the images to be sure it is the same animal all along?

EJH: With CTDS data, we do not recommend estimating group density and group size, because group size may be underestimated. We recommend treating individuals rather than groups as the unit of observation. The assumption that observations are independent is already severely violated due to small t and the inclusion of multiple observations from the same animal during a single pass through the area monitored by a CT. The data you use to estimate detectability and abundance should have a separate row and observation of distance for each animal in the FOV of an image included in the dataset. This should not affect estimation of t because they are all detected at the same time (no time interval between these detections). "Intervals" of 0 seconds for > 1 animal in the same image should not be included in data used to estimate t.

For example for wild pig, sometimes, I have one individual entering the FOV then going out, then maybe 5 seconds later a second individual entering the FOV.  And then the two individuals again enter the FOV at the same time. Since I filtered for only images with 1 individual, I won't get that images with 2 individuals. But I do know in my case it is 2 different events because later on I will have those 2 individuals with all their babies for example. How do I deal with that?

EJH: Because the pigs travel in groups, it will be difficult to separate retrigger times of animals that remain stationary in front of the camera for a few seconds from consecutive triggers from different animals. That could make defining an appropriate truncation time difficult because distributions of retrigger times from the same animals, and from different animals, will overlap. This might require you to take the "direct approach" and filter for pictures belonging to the same animal. Don't filter for images with only 1 animal.

>
> I see in the csv file that they are four columns that I do not have in my record table: delta.time.secs, Beh_numeric_event, ID, EventID. I assume the delta.time.secs can be obtained using the package camtrapR and a threshold of 5 minutes for indepedent event can be used (everything less than 5 minutes is considered the same event or same individual and therefore will calculate the delta.time.secs between each photos). However in my data analysis I used a threshold of 60 minutes to filter for independent events, does it mean I need to use the same in this case? Also what does Beh_numeric_event represent? Are the two last columns used in the csv file of importance for the analysis? I assume the interval used in the R script is the delta.time.secs column.

EJH: Sorry I don't quite follow here. We include non-independent observations in CTDS data, and in the data used to estimate t. I also didn't conduct the analysis so would have to check on those column labels.

>
> Another question is how to incorporate that "mean time interval between triggers' into my data analysis. If we take for example the siamese fireback in my dataset (pheasant), which reacted to the camera by getting very close to the camera and staring at it for long period of time. I have the effort in days for each cameras deployed, and based on the activity histogram, we estimate the daily time activity from 5:45 am to 18:15 am, so 12 hours and 30 minutes daily. So the daily Tk is 12.5 hours and then we need to multiply it by the numbers of days camera were active and then divide by t, which is the time interval between snapshots, so 2 seconds here. I assume therefore I would only change this 't' and replace by the one obtained following the methodology from the article.

EJH: Multiple issues here. Observations of reacting animals should be censored. If animals are only active from 5:45 through 18:15, you can set daily Tk to 12.5 hours (in seconds) and multiply by camera days and divide by t to get temporal effort. However, this is insufficient to account for the effect of animal activity on abundance estimates unless animals are continuously active for all of those 12.5 hours. You should still estimate activity level (following Rowcliffe et al.) within those 12.5 hours and include this proportion when estimating abundance (A-hat in Eq 2 of the article). We estimate activity level within the time included in our survey duration (Tk). In practice, it's often simpler to set daily Tk to 24 hours and estimate activity level over 24 hours. For most animals, activity level over 24 hours is < 0.5 (they rest for about half the day but also rest during the half of the day when they are active).

EJH: Yes, when estimating effort we will divide by t, and your 2 seconds would be replaced by estimated t.

> But what about all the distance estimations I did at the interval of 2 sec on my images for each species ? In my case, I filtered for all images in the record table that finished by an even number for the time and only estimated the distances for these images.
> In the article, to do the data analysis, the first photo of each photo series was used a snapshot moment. Do I therefore need to review this step and do distance estimation for the first photo of each photo series? In my case, the settings used are the following: "Cameras were programmed to operate all day and to record one photo at each activation, with the minimum triggering interval between activations (0.6 seconds)." Or if I found for example a t of 6 seconds, do I need to take only images in the data analysis every 6 seconds ?

EJH: If your cameras were programmed to record a single image when triggered, and performed well enough to detect animals after < 2 seconds (i.e., if recovery time in the field really was < 2 seconds), and if many (non-reacting) animals contribute more than one observation of distance with t = 2 seconds, then perhaps you don't need the methods described in this article? You could use predetermined moments 2 seconds apart and select the images that most closely align with those moments. If recovery times are reliably short (< t) then they won't cause bias. Retrigger times would only be a serious issue if animals frequently remained stationary in the FOV such that they went undetected at snapshot moments, but you could check for that in your data and correct the data instead of applying these methods.

Filtering using even numbers sounds like it could be effective, provided you're not dropping observations because time stamps are not rounded to the nearest second. E.g. we don't want to discard both images if they occur at 1.5 and 2.1 seconds, we'd chose the one at 2.1 which closely aligns to a predetermined snapshot moments.

EJH: If you use an estimated t, you would include all images of non-reacting animals in the data used to estimate abundance. Some would be < estimated t apart, but that's fine because it's a mean across short and long intervals. So, if estimated t is 6 seconds, you should set t to 6 seconds not 2 seconds, but do not "take only images in the data analysis every 6 seconds".

EJH: If you can use a "checked data set" (consecutive images of only the same animals, excluding reacting animals) and find that estimated t is < 2 seconds, I don't think you need these methods. Just use t = 2 seconds and select the images that fall closest to predetermined moments for estimating the detection function and abundance.

>
> Sorry for all the questions... Hopefully I was clear enough in my explanation...
>
> Thank you for all your help,
>
> Best regards,
>
> Emeline

Hello,

I'm currently in the final phase of my analysis, aiming to estimate the abundance of small cetaceans.

I've attached the survey design (somewhat random, but the essential is there). There are a total of 21 blocks covering an large study area. It's a vessel-based line transect survey equipped with a towed hydrophone array. The vessel operated continuously day and night, resulting in some transects surveyed only with the acoustic platform (i.e., during nighttime), others with only the visual platform (i.e., in shallow waters), and some where both platforms were used.

In previous studies, I employed an MRDS analysis on transects using both platforms to estimate g(0) (see paper Ollier et al., 2023: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2023.1244474). I obtained g(0) values for different platform types:

- Acoustic platform only: g(0) = 0.32
- Visual platform only: g(0) = 0.29

mult <- list(creation= data.frame(rate=0.52, SE=0))
 ds(         data,
                truncation= TD,
                transect = "line",
                formula=as.formula(~SeaState),
                key="hn",
                multipliers = mult)

In this case, is there a function to apply the g(0) value according to the type of transects we have here, and can this work with the dht2/ds function?

Any guidance or direction would be immensely appreciated.

Thank you in advance

Best

Camille

Camille

Congratulations on your paper. Thanks for the figure describing your design, that makes the question quite clear.

Unfortunately, the answer is not so clear. There is the ability in the dht2​ function of the Distance​ package to provide stratum (or block)-specific multipliers, but there is not the ability to work with multipliers that vary by transect.

We haven't provided an worked example showing the use of stratum-specific multipliers, so I provide one below.
library(Distance)
data(minke)
bystrata <- ds(minke, key="hr", truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)
# fictitious g(0) and standard errors just for demonstration
g0north <- 0.9
g0north.se <http://g0north.se> <- 0.1
g0south <- 0.2
g0south.se <http://g0south.se> <- 0.05

myg0 <- data.frame(Region.Label=c("North", "South"),
                   rate=c(g0north, g0south),
                   SE=c(g0north.se <http://g0north.se>, g0south.se <http://g0south.se>))
g0multiplier <- list(creation=myg0)

minke.with.g0 <- dht2(ddf = bystrata,
                      flatfile = minke,
                      strat_formula = ~Region.Label,
                      multipliers = g0multiplier)

# stratum-specific abundance without g0 adjustment
print(bystrata$dht$individuals$N)

# stratum-specific abundance after applying stratum-specific g0 multipliers
print(minke.with.g0, report = "abundance")
# Note northern stratum abundance estimate after g0 is 10% larger (g0(north)=0.9)
# but southern stratum abundance estimate is 5X larger (g0(south)=0.2)

I don't know if you want block-specific abundance estimates, or simply an overall estimate. If it is the latter, you might consider reorganising your data such that the "strata" conform to the platform type. Then you can match the multiplier with the stratum type and use dht2​ to produce platform-specific estimates. The overall density estimate would be a weighted average, weighting by effort associated with the different platforms (stratification="replicate" for the dht2​ argument). That's a bit messy and I'm not confident it will give you what you want, but it is an approximation.

Remember there is uncertainty in your g(0) estimates that must be included as part of the multiplier data frame (as shown in code above) to properly propagate uncertainty into your abundance estimates. Quoting here from your paper abstract:
> We tested the models with two key functions. With a hazard-rate key function, the g(0) was estimated at 0.52 (CV=21.0%) for both platforms combined, 0.29 (CV=25.6%) for the visual platform and 0.32 (CV=25.1%) for the acoustic platform.
Remember to convert the CVs into standard errors: SE=\hat{g0} * CV  where CV is a proportion not a percentage.

Adding to Eric’s comments, it’s a tricky one because some of your plots are well covered by the points, and it would be fine to treat the point as the sample units, while others just have a single line of points through the plot.  If plots are very homogeneous, it might not be unreasonable to treat each point as a unit, but to note this issue when writing up.  I guess you could try bootstrapping, once with plots as the sample units and once with points, and see if the 2 options lead to appreciably different inference.

For the plots with just a single line of points, you could regard your inference to be restricted to a strip of width 400m centred on the line, in which case you could arguably justify using points as units.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Niccolò

Welcome to the group.

The "Area" to specify in your analysis is the size of the portion of the earth over which you are willing to make inference about the density of the deer you are studying.  This means the places where you did deploy your thermal imager are representative of what greater region; remember you are conducting sampling—you do not visit all points in your region of interest.

In your question you state "... camera, in the open fields..." I therefore infer that you only placed your imager in open fields (not in forests). If that is true, you should not make inference about deer in forests because you did not sample there. I think that excludes your option #1.

To differentiate between options #2 and #3, you need to decide whether your imager placement was randomly distributed in open fields, such that you can say the locations of the imager were representative of all the open fields. It seems (from the blue and yellow lines) that placement of the imager was not completely random, but rather some sort of track was followed. Open fields remote from tracks were not sampled, hence would be excluded from the region about which you can safely make inference. I suspect the answer to you question will be option #3, but that depends upon how the blue tracks (and subsequent imager placements) were determined.

It is customary for the delineation of the study area (and hence its size) to be determine prior to the collection of data, rather than after data collection. By defining at the outset of the study, the region of interest, the specification of a study design, complete with a method of random placement of the point transects (as in your imager situation) follows from the region over which you wish to make inference.

messages.subject: Two-stage count model, ML, or Bayesian for multi-species point count data?
messages.subject_clean: Two-stage count model, ML, or Bayesian for multi-species point count data?
messages.body_plain:
Dear DS community,
I want to assess the impact of farming practice and of small-scale habitat/native vegetation patches on the abundance of ~100 bird species (for some analyses expressed in relation to their abundances in the forest). I'm trying to figure out how information can best be shared between species and get the most precise estimates.
In occupancy modelling, a Bayesian approach is very common, but seems to be less so for distance sampling (- is there a reason for this?). I take from this blog (Model-based inference analysis from Buckland et al. (2015) (distancesampling.org) <https://examples.distancesampling.org/book-bobwhite/bobwhite.html#defining-the-likelihood-function>) that I ultimately have three options (two-stage count model, maximum likelihood, or Bayesian) but I struggle to find what would be most suitable in my case.

I have 25 forest squares, 13 natural farming squares, and 13 chemical farming squares. Each square is 500m x 500m and contains 4 systematically arranged point count locations, 200m apart and 150m from the square edge. I visited each point count 4 times: winter 2022, summer 2022, winter 2023, summer 2023. The natural & chemcial farming squares span a gradient in the percentage of habitat patches embedded in the square. I counted all bird species I saw or heard, so that's a bit over 100 species. Whilst some were very common, others (especially forest specialists) were rare.

Initially, I was planning on conducting a two-stage count model: For species with at least 40 observations, I'd fit species-specific detection functions. For those with fewer observations, I'd group species into detectability groups based on taxonomic, dietary, and behavioural characteristics (obtained from AVONET). For each species or group, I'd then fit detection functions where I'd consider three models for each species or species group: a detection function with (1) land use type (farming vs forest) as a covariate, (2) the proportion of closed habitat (surrounding each point) as a covariate, and (3) no covariates. In each case, I'd test the following key functions and adjustments half-normal and hazard-rate with cosine adjustment, half-normal with hermite polynomial adjustment, and hazard-rate with simple polynomial adjustment. For the group-level detection functions, I'd include species as a covariate in each model. I'd then fit linear mixed models to the observed count data, seperately for each species, with the estimated effective area as an offset and a nested random effect with square identity as a random term and farming practice and the percentage of habitat patches as predictor variables (and using bca bootstrapping to get CIs).
(I'd then also fit bird density-crop yield functions, seperately for each farming practice for each species following Phalan et al 2011 <https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1208742>, where forest is zero yielding).

However, I feel that information is not shared as effectively between species as it could (should?) be when it comes to estimating square-level density for each species & modelling the effect of farming pratice & habitat patches. I am thus wondering whether a ML or Bayesian approach would give me more precision in my estimates (ie increase my ability to detect effects if there are any) and/or save me time, but I am unsure of how to find out whether either of them would be suitable and how this code <https://examples.distancesampling.org/book-bobwhite/bobwhite.html#defining-the-likelihood-function> could be best updated for multiple species (presumably by adding species as a random term as well as some trait characteristics?).

Some guidance on this would be greatly appreciated. I haven't found any examples of the ML or Bayesian approach in a similar context.

Many thanks,
Iris

Several issues associated with your question.
First the error message. Your data file contains five values for Region.Label​. The software is checking that the transect length associated with transects within each Region.Label​ are the same. That is not the case with your data, because you have the 2022 and 2023 data within the same Region.Label​. For example, Transect 1 in Region Mota C.​ has Effort=5​ for 2022, but the same transect has Effort=3.8​ for 2023.
Solution: Recast your data such that the Regions are Mota22​, Mota23​, Belmonte22​, Belmonte23​, etc. This will solve your error message, but it will highlight that there are unlikely to be sufficient detections to support unique detection function models for each of your location x season combinations.
Number of detections by location (ignoring year):
MOTAC=20, BELMONTE=8, QUERO=51, LONGAR=28, P.MUNOZ=16
this suggests you will struggle to produce defensible estimates by location (ignoring year) without the use of location as a covariate
when you truncate to a reasonable distance, e.g. 100m, the 123 total detections is reduced to ~80
Distribution of detection distances will make it difficult to fit a detection function model. Half-normal key function models will lack fit and hazard rate key function models will predict unrealistically large estimates of density
Of the 123 detections in the data set, over 1/3 of the detections are at distances <10m

Adding to Eric’s comments, as he notes, movement is likely to be a major issue, unless you had a protocol to deal with this. Movement independent of the observer generates too many detections close to the line unless it is slow relative to observer speed (if for example you were using a vehicle or drone). However, it would be unlikely to generate the spike at zero that your data show. That might occur if for example your transects were tracks through forest, and kites were often seen crossing the track ahead of the observer. It might also occur if observers were not trained to get good estimates of distance from the line, and often recorded birds that were ahead of them as on the line. Another possibility is that  missing distance estimates were recorded as zeros.

Polina

That is quite an ambitious survey. The question about how to organise your data is tied to the design of your survey and the estimates you wish (robustly) produce. Your email covers survey design, data organisation and (tacitly) modelling strategy. Our discussion may take a few iterations to arrive at a solution.

I understand that in a perfect situation, you would like to produce estimates for each (let's say 20) species in each of 16 forest fragments in each of three years. That would amount to 960 estimates. I suspect that is beyond the reach of your data unless you make (untestable) assumptions about detectability; i.e. detectability is the same across some combination of years/fragments/species. Using pooled detection function to produce estimates at lower levels of data organisation is likely to produce biased estimates. In your situation, if you pool data across fragments for fitting detection functions, then try to produce fragment-specific estimates, those estimates are likely to be biased. This is discussed in this paper
Rexstad, E., Buckland, S., Marshall, L., & Borchers, D. (2023). Pooling robustness in distance sampling: Avoiding bias when there is unmodelled heterogeneity. Ecology and Evolution, 13(1), e9684.  https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.9684

>From the survey design information you provided, there are 74 point transects spread across 16 fragments; resulting in an average of 4.6 points per fragment. That is a low level of replication for fragment-specific estimates; we recommend a level of replication closer to 15-20 transects per stratum. Is there some natural combining of adjacent fragments (giving rise to new geographic strata) that would be sensible for producing meaningful estimates with an increased number of spatial replicate points? For example, if it makes sense to merge 4 nearby fragments into a single stratum, you would increase the number of transects to ~18. There may also be beneficial effects of increasing number of detections per stratum. The answer to this question will have consequences for your data entry.

For the first two types of estimates you want (species within fragments, species over entire study area) you make no mention of how you intend to treat year. Assuming you want year-specificity in this, you could consider merging year and fragment into strata (Begovo20, Begovo21, Begovo22, etc; similar to what you have in your second screenshot).

Your comments in your last paragraph:
if you visited each point twice during the year, then Effort would be recorded as 2. It is sensible to pool detections across visits within year.
you are right, creating projects specific to each species is probably a bad idea for two reasons
it is more work to duplication the design information in each project (you can use the data filter to subset the entire dataset for separate species)
as you noted, if species are not detected at some points, effort can be misrepresented producing positive bias in your estimates.

As you can see, there are many issues embedded in your email. One step you have already begun (you noted the number of species for which you have >50 detections) is to summarise your data before entering them into Distance for Windows. In your spreadsheet, you could produce tabulations of the number of detections by species, year, fragment (perhaps with various spatial definitions of fragments—see my earlier comment regarding this). This will inform your decisions regarding the amount of support your detection function models might have, having consequences for the strength of your inferences.

Now you can see the likely iterative nature of this conversation. There is likely compromise to be made between the level of inference you wish to make (960 independent estimates) and the support for that degree of inference in your data. If you want to continue this dialogue, we could carry on off-list and you could come back to the list with final conclusions.
